'''''Alocasia brisbanensis''''', commonly known as '''cunjevoi''',{{efn|name=note1|The term "cunjevoi" also refers to a [[Pyura stolonifera|marine animal]]}} '''elephant ear''', '''native lily''' or '''spoon lily''',{{R|DESQLD|APNI|RFK}} is a species of plant in the family [[Araceae]] native to [[rainforest]]s of eastern [[Australia]]. The common name "cunjevoi" derives from the [[Yugambeh–Bundjalung languages|Bundjalung language]] of northern [[New South Wales]].{{R|SLOQ}} It has been cultivated for its large tropical leaves and the heavily scented flowers.{{R|RFK}}

==Description==
[[File:Alocasia brisbanensis (Bailey) Domin (AM AK302022-3).jpg|thumb|left|Leaf detail]]
''Alocasia brisbanensis'' has very large, spade-shaped, veined leaves on long, fleshy, purplish brown to green, [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]s that are {{cvt|1.1|m}} long. The plant grows to a height of {{cvt|1.5|m}} to {{cvt|1.8|m}}. Leaves are [[sagittate]] to ovate-sagittate, around {{cvt|70|cm}} long and {{cvt|60|cm}} wide. They are glossy green in colour, glabrous.{{R|NET}} Backside lobes have acute to rectangular, marginally rounded tips.<ref name=aroid/>

Stretched 'oil dots' are visible along the veinlets of the leaves.{{R|RFK}} New [[Shoot (botany)|shoot]]s grow concurrently with the [[inflorescence]], without a rest period. Stem is prostrate to erect, {{cvt|13|cm}} in diameter, arrayed in the brown remains of spent leaf bases.<ref name="aroid">{{Cite web |title=ALOCASIA BRISBANENSIS |url=https://www.aroidpedia.com/journal/alocasia-brisbanensis |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=Aroidpedia |language=en-US |archive-date=18 May 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260518084218/https://www.aroidpedia.com/journal/alocasia-brisbanensis |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Inflorescence===   
The [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] is just about as long as the petioles. The [[spathe]] is around {{cvt|25|cm}} long, confined around a third of the length from the base, and is pointed at the tip and open by one side. The limb is ovate to lanceolate, spoon-like (seldom crooked), generally green, which wilts away. The [[Spadix (botany)|spadix]] is somewhat shorter than the spathe, dwindling, and is extremely fragrant. Male flowers are typically straight with up to 40 consolidated [[anthers]].{{R|NET}} There is a distinct flowering peak in December and January, though there are flowering and fruiting collections from all months, except the winter.<ref name=aroid/>

The [[pollen]] is white or translucent, and the [[Stigma (botany)|stigma]] is three-lobed.{{R|RFK}} The perfumed, summer [[flowers]] are greenish-cream in colour, and similar to an [[arum lily]]. The [[ovoid]], 8–15 mm long red fruits, with a pink or red [[pericarp]], follow the flowering.{{R|RFK|WRIGLEY}} Fruits split open lengthwise when mature.<ref name=aroid/> Seeds are one or two per fruit, about 6–7 mm long. The [[embryo]] is about 5 mm long.{{R|RFK}} [[Ovary]] is pale green, and female zone contains 120 [[pistil]]s.<ref name=aroid/>

Fruit is eaten by [[Lewin's honeyeater]]s, [[regent bowerbird]]s, [[brush-turkey]]s, [[eastern water dragon]]s and [[Victoria's riflebird]]s.{{R|RFK}}<ref name=aroid/>

==Distribution==
[[File:Alocasia brisbanensis Maiala National Park Mt Glorious 1980s IMG 0111.jpg|thumb|At [[D'Aguilar National Park]] in Queensland]]
It is found on tropical, subtropical, and warm temperate rainforest margins at low altitudes, and as an [[understorey]] herbaceous plant in moist, shaded to partial shaded areas, such as creeks and wetlands.<ref>[https://www.forestheart.com.au/articles/focus-on-flora-cunjevoi-alocasia-brisbanensis Focus on Flora: Cunjevoi - Alocasia brisbanensis] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251127045316/https://www.forestheart.com.au/articles/focus-on-flora-cunjevoi-alocasia-brisbanensis |date=27 November 2025 }} Forest Heart ecoNursery. Retrieved 9 October 2025.</ref> It thrives in [[pleiotrophic]] soils, along creek lines and moist forest grounds, such as [[Coastal Swamp Oak Forest]]s.<ref name=aroid/>

It is native to [[Queensland]].<ref name="aroid" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Alocasia brisbanensis |url=https://wildnet.science-data.qld.gov.au/taxon-detail?taxon_id=9788&tab=0&backQuery=location_search_by%3Darea%26taxon_name%3DAlocasia%2Bbrisbanensis%26advanced%3Dfalse%26tab%3D0 |access-date=2026-07-06 |website=WildNet |publisher=Queensland Government}}</ref>

In [[New South Wales]], it is found mainly in coastal areas and [[Disturbance (ecology)|disturbed areas]], north from the [[Illawarra]] district, inland to [[Dorrigo, New South Wales|Dorrigo]] and upper [[Clarence River (New South Wales)|Clarence River]].{{R|NET}} Its [[altitudinal range]] is from near sea level to {{cvt|1000|m}}.{{R|RFK}}

==Cultivation==
It is cultivated as a [[houseplant]] and a [[garden plant]] namely for its large, exotic looking leaves and perfumed flowers. It thrives in bright sunlight when grown indoors, though the afternoon sun can bleach the leaves. In the garden, it does well in partial shade, though since it is a [[tropical plant]] it can be sensitive to cold or dry conditions and it requires high humidity levels to flourish. In the winter, the plant goes through a [[dormancy]] period. The plant benefits from a [[fertiliser]] in the growing season for nourishment. [[Mealybug]]s, [[spider mite]]s and [[aphid]]s are pests that commonly affect the plant.<ref>[https://www.thejunglecollective.com.au/alocasia-brisbanensis-cunjevoi-elephant-ear-plant-care-tips/?srsltid=AfmBOoqN51jOm9lxHPORVSEyeN-C4caeM9RuX4XXgUPzbsVszStrEBPP Alocasia Brisbanensis – Cunjevoi Elephant Ear – Plant Care Tips] The Jungle Collective Nursery. Retrieved 9 October 2025.</ref>

==Chemistry==
The plant is poisonous, and contact with the [[sap]] can lead to skin and eye irritation due to the presence of needle-like crystals of [[Calcium oxalate]].{{R|RFK}} Eating any part of the plant causes immediate pain, a burning sensation and swelling of the lips, tongue and mouth. A small number of children have died as a result of eating parts of the plant.{{R|CHQ}}

A percentage of people believe that newly-cut leaf stalks or stems of the plant will act as an [[antidote]] for the sting of the [[Stinging Tree]], relieving the stinging pain.{{R|RFK}}
